opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find promising is that when you have abundant compute, you can ask different kinds of questions. In many research settings you design around scarcity: you pick the one experiment you can afford and hope your intuition was right. With a compute-intensive approach you can run a lot of variations in parallel, sweep the design space more honestly, and let the empirical results correct your intuitions instead of the other way around.

There's also a tight feedback loop between the research and the systems underneath it. If you're working close to the hardware and the software stack, you see where the real bottlenecks are, whether that's memory bandwidth, communication between GPUs, or data pipelines. Research ideas that look elegant on paper but don't scale get filtered out quickly, and ideas that do scale get pushed much further than they otherwise would. I think that grounding is valuable.

Another part is that scale itself reveals behavior you just don't see in small experiments. Some capabilities, and some failure modes, only show up when you train larger models or run longer. If you never have the compute to reach that regime, you're partly guessing about what matters. So having the resources to actually go there and measure things is, to me, a big advantage.

That said, I don't think compute replaces good ideas. The most exciting work happens when strong intuition about what's worth trying meets the resources to test it rigorously. Compute amplifies good research taste; it doesn't substitute for it. That combination is what I find most promising.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention the joke that NVIDIA pursues compute-intensive research to sell more GPUs.

r002.rationale: It says scale can reveal behaviors and capabilities, but does not identify past improvements from scaling data and GPU resources as grounds for optimism.

r003.rationale: It describes running many variations, but does not suggest that simple brute-force approaches have aesthetic appeal.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find promising is actually pretty simple: they've made a bet that scale is a research instrument, not just a product. A lot of labs treat compute as a cost to be managed. NVIDIA treats it as a lens. When you can afford to run the same experiment at ten different sizes, you stop guessing about whether an idea works and start seeing how it behaves as it grows. That changes the kind of questions you can ask.

The second thing is that they sit at the intersection of hardware and research, so their researchers don't have to treat the hardware as fixed. If something is slow, the answer isn't always "find a cleverer algorithm." Sometimes the answer is "change the chip," or "change the interconnect," and those conversations actually happen inside the same company. That feedback loop between what researchers want to try and what the silicon can do is rare. Most of us live on one side of that wall.

And then there's the honest part, which is that a lot of what looked like deep insight in this field over the last decade turned out to be "we had more compute than the last group." That sounds cynical, but it's actually useful to know. It means if you can push the frontier of what's physically runnable, you're going to find things that nobody could have seen before, almost by default. NVIDIA is one of the few places structurally positioned to keep doing that.

The caveat I'd add is that compute-intensive research has a failure mode, which is that you stop looking for ideas that are cheap. The most interesting work usually comes from people who have the big machines but still ask, "what's the smallest version of this that would tell me something?" The promising version of NVIDIA's approach is the one where scale is used to verify, not to replace thinking.

r003.rationale: The response argues that more compute can reveal how ideas behave at scale, but does not suggest that simple brute-force approaches have aesthetic appeal.

astra-6.text:
What I find promising is that more compute can change the way you do research. You can test more ideas, run richer simulations, and get feedback faster. That can make questions that once seemed impractical worth exploring.

But the key is what you do with that capacity. If you pair it with good research questions and careful experiments, compute becomes a tool for discovery. Simply making an experiment bigger doesn’t necessarily make it more informative.
